name: Big hair / bouffant

card.summary: A voluminous, teased hairstyle that raises hair high on the crown and puffs it around the head, used to add height, soften the face and frame it with volume.
card.aka: Bouffant, teased hair, beehive (taller variant), big hair
card.note: Teasing and heavy hairspray are typical of the style; no studies have examined its effect on perceived attractiveness.

quick.overview:
A bouffant is a puffy, rounded hairstyle with the hair lifted high on the head and usually covering or framing the ears and sides. The name comes from the French bouffante, from bouffer, meaning to puff up.

For appearance, the style adds height at the crown and width around the head, which can visually lengthen a short or round face and frame the features with volume. It has recurred as a retro look from the 1950s and 60s to today, and its taller form is the beehive.
quick.how: The hair at the crown is backcombed, or teased, into a loose pile, smooth front hair is combed over it, and the ends are styled and set with hairspray or lacquer. A wiglet or mesh cushion can add height, and a rattail comb is used to lift the hair back into shape because brushing would flatten it. Stylists also vary it with bangs or a hair fall.
quick.risks: The style carries no medical risk of its own, but repeated teasing, strong hold products and heavy styling are the practical considerations stylists mention for hair upkeep. It takes time to set and is affected by weather and sleep.

lead: A bouffant is a puffy, rounded hairstyle in which hair is raised high on the head, usually covering the ears or hanging at the sides. The word comes from the French bouffante, from bouffer, to puff or fluff up.[1] It is a variant of the eighteenth-century pouf worn in aristocratic wigs decorated with feathers, ribbons, flowers and jewellery.[1]

Its appeal for appearance is volume: height at the crown and fullness at the sides change the silhouette of the head and frame the face. The style signalled upper-class status in its early history and later became linked to 1950s and 1960s domestic life, girl groups and rockabilly, returning repeatedly as a retro look.[1]

The revival is credited to British stylist Raymond Bessone in the 1950s, and Jacqueline Kennedy's low bouffant bob increased its popularity in the United States in the 1960s.[1] Taller beehives were worn by Dusty Springfield and by girl groups such as the Supremes and the Ronettes, and later by Amy Winehouse.[1]

angle.text: Raising and puffing the hair adds apparent height and fullness, which people use to balance facial proportions or add glamour. The effect is immediate and lasts until the hair is washed or brushed out.

paras: Voluminous styles returned in the late Victorian era among high society, and Charles Dana Gibson's Gibson Girl, from about 1891, popularised the bouffant in the Belle Epoque until the First World War.[1] In the Edwardian period it stayed a symbol of aristocracy, supported by waxes, fixatives and hairpieces, before bobs and the flapper style replaced it.[1]

It came back in the 1950s with the rockabilly look and became a common style for American housewives in the 1960s; sales of hair rollers and hairspray rose with it.[1] The beehive revived in the 2000s with Amy Winehouse, and the bouffant and pompadour came back in the 2010s under hipster and retro influence, worn by singers such as Adele and Rihanna.[1]

The base is made by backcombing hair on top of the head into a loose pile, combing smooth front hair over it and styling the outer ends in various ways, with hairspray or lacquer holding the shape.[1] A wiglet or nylon mesh cushion can add crown height, and bangs or a hair fall may be added.[1]

No studies found. Medical journals use the word bouffant for a different item, a surgical cap worn in operating rooms, and a body of literature compares bouffant caps with skull caps for surgical site infection;[2][3] that research concerns the cap and not the hairstyle.

timeline.event: The Gibson Girl popularises voluminous hair in the Belle Epoque.[1]
Raymond Bessone is credited with the bouffant revival, nicknamed teasy-weasy.[1]
Jacqueline Kennedy's low bouffant and the beehive spread through girl groups.[1]
